# Exercise 5.3 — Decision trees that overfit {#sec-decision-trees}


:::: {.web-only}
Every cell on this page is a real R or Python cell, run against
`data/diabetes.csv` with the same split as @sec-classification-metrics.
::::

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Fit a classification tree, draw it, and read a prediction off the drawing
  for one patient without running any code.
- Produce a model with perfect training accuracy and show, in the same cell,
  that it is worse than useless on held-out patients.
- Choose `tree_depth` and `min_n` by grid search over resampled training data,
  and say why the test set took no part in that choice.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-classification-metrics left a logistic regression with a test AUC around
0.8. Its boundary is one straight line in eight dimensions, which is a strong
assumption about how diabetes risk is organised. A tree makes almost no
assumption: it splits the data on one variable at a time and keeps going. That
freedom is the attraction, and it is also the whole problem — a tree allowed to
keep going will eventually isolate every training patient in a leaf of their
own, at which point it is a lookup table for data you already have.

This is the first model in the booklet where the honest evaluation and the
flattering one differ by thirty points.

## Worked example — a tree, drawn

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 7
library(tidymodels); library(readr); library(rpart.plot)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv") |>
  dplyr::mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("pos", "neg")))

set.seed(123)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.7, strata = diabetes)
train <- training(split); test <- testing(split)

tree_fit <- decision_tree() |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

tree_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot(extra = 101, roundint = FALSE)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 8
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, recall_score, roc_auc_score

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
X = diabetes.drop(columns="diabetes")
y = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3,
                                          random_state=123, stratify=y)

tree_fit = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=123).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
plot_tree(tree_fit, max_depth=2, feature_names=list(X.columns),
          class_names=["neg", "pos"], filled=True, fontsize=7, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Top two levels only — the full tree has "
             f"{tree_fit.get_n_leaves()} leaves")
plt.show()
```
:::

Each box holds the rule, the counts of `pos` and `neg` training patients
reaching it, and the share of the training rows it covers. A prediction is one
walk from the root to a leaf; nothing is multiplied, nothing is exponentiated,
and a clinician can audit the path. That transparency is the main clinical
argument for trees.

Now score it on both sets.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
tree_scores <- function(fit, label) {
  one <- function(dat, set) {
    p <- augment(fit, dat)
    tibble::tibble(
      model = label, set = set,
      accuracy = accuracy(p, diabetes, .pred_class)$.estimate,
      sens     = sens(p, diabetes, .pred_class)$.estimate,
      spec     = yardstick::specificity(p, diabetes, .pred_class)$.estimate,
      auc      = roc_auc(p, diabetes, .pred_pos)$.estimate)
  }
  dplyr::bind_rows(one(train, "train"), one(test, "test"))
}

n_leaves <- function(fit) sum(extract_fit_engine(fit)$frame$var == "<leaf>")

tree_scores(tree_fit, "rpart defaults")
n_leaves(tree_fit)
```

## Python

```{python}
def tree_scores(fit, label):
    rows = []
    for name, Xs, ys in [("train", X_tr, y_tr), ("test", X_te, y_te)]:
        pred = fit.predict(Xs)
        rows.append({"model": label, "set": name,
                     "accuracy": accuracy_score(ys, pred),
                     "sens": recall_score(ys, pred),
                     "spec": recall_score(1 - ys, 1 - pred),
                     "auc": roc_auc_score(ys, fit.predict_proba(Xs)[:, 1])})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

print(tree_scores(tree_fit, "sklearn defaults"))
tree_fit.get_n_leaves()
```
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The two defaults are not the same model, and this is not a bug in either
`decision_tree()` in R hands `rpart` its own defaults, which include a
complexity parameter of 0.01: the tree is pruned as it is built, and you get
about ten leaves and a train-test accuracy gap of four points.
`DecisionTreeClassifier()` in Python has no such stopping rule and grows until
every leaf is pure: 110 leaves, fourteen levels deep, training accuracy of
exactly 1.000, and a test accuracy below the majority-class rule.

Both libraries are behaving as documented. The lesson is that "I used the
default tree" names two different models, and that the published accuracy of a
tree tells you nothing until you know how it was stopped. Print the number of
leaves whenever you fit one.
:::

## Worked example — the same thing in R, on purpose

To see the Python default's behaviour in R, remove the pruning: a complexity
parameter of zero, leaves allowed down to two patients, depth up to thirty.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
deep_fit <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0, min_n = 2, tree_depth = 30) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

tree_scores(deep_fit, "unconstrained")
n_leaves(deep_fit)
```

## Python

```{python}
# Nothing to do: this is what DecisionTreeClassifier() already did above.
tree_fit.get_depth(), tree_fit.get_n_leaves()
```
:::

Training accuracy 1.000. Training AUC 1.000. A model that has not made a single
mistake on the data it was shown, and that you would present to no one.

## Task 2 — Stop guessing: search the grid

Trying values by hand does not scale past two hyperparameters, and choosing
among them by test-set performance would spend the test set. The alternative is
to split the **training** rows again, several ways, and score every candidate
on rows it did not see within each split.

::: {.callout-note}
## Five folds, and why the test set is still untouched
`vfold_cv(train, v = 5)` cuts the training rows into five parts, fits on four
and scores on the fifth, five times, and averages. Every number used to choose
hyperparameters comes from training rows. The test set is opened once, at the
end of Task 3, and never again. Tuning on the test set is not a small sin: it
converts your held-out estimate into a training estimate, silently.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
tree_spec <- decision_tree(tree_depth = tune(), min_n = tune(),
                           cost_complexity = ______) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("classification")

tree_grid <- grid_regular(tree_depth(range = c(2L, 10L)),
                          min_n(range = c(5L, 40L)),
                          cost_complexity(range = c(-3, -1)),
                          levels = 3)
nrow(tree_grid)

set.seed(123)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = diabetes)

tree_wf  <- workflow() |> add_model(tree_spec) |> add_formula(diabetes ~ .)
tree_res <- tune_grid(tree_wf, resamples = ______, grid = tree_grid,
                      metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy))

show_best(tree_res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 5)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
A hyperparameter you want the grid to choose is not given a number. The second
blank is the object holding the five resamples.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
tree_spec <- decision_tree(tree_depth = tune(), min_n = tune(),
                           cost_complexity = tune()) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("classification")

tree_grid <- grid_regular(tree_depth(range = c(2L, 10L)),
                          min_n(range = c(5L, 40L)),
                          cost_complexity(range = c(-3, -1)),
                          levels = 3)
nrow(tree_grid)

set.seed(123)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = diabetes)

tree_wf  <- workflow() |> add_model(tree_spec) |> add_formula(diabetes ~ .)
tree_res <- tune_grid(tree_wf, resamples = folds, grid = tree_grid,
                      metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy))

show_best(tree_res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 5)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
param_grid = {"max_depth": [2, 6, 10],
              "min_samples_leaf": [5, 20, 40],
              "ccp_alpha": [0.001, 0.01]}

search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=123),
                      param_grid,
                      cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=123),
                      scoring=______).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(search.best_params_, round(search.best_score_, 3))
print(np.round([search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"].min(),
                search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"].max()], 3))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
param_grid = {"max_depth": [2, 6, 10],
              "min_samples_leaf": [5, 20, 40],
              "ccp_alpha": [0.001, 0.01]}

search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=123),
                      param_grid,
                      cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=123),
                      scoring="roc_auc").fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(search.best_params_, round(search.best_score_, 3))
print(np.round([search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"].min(),
                search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"].max()], 3))
```
:::
:::
:::

Look at the `std_err` column in R's `show_best()` output, or at the spread
between the best and worst grid point in Python. The whole grid spans
about 0.06–0.10 of AUC and the standard error of each estimate is about
0.02–0.03. The top few rows are not distinguishable from one another, so treat
`select_best()` as picking one of several equally good settings rather than as
finding the right one.

## Task 3 — Finalise, and open the test set once

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
best_tree  <- select_best(tree_res, metric = "roc_auc")
best_tree

final_fit  <- finalize_workflow(tree_wf, ______) |> fit(data = train)
final_scores <- tree_scores(final_fit, "tuned")
final_scores
n_leaves(final_fit)

check_beats_prevalence(final_scores$accuracy[final_scores$set == "test"],
                       test$diabetes)
check_overfit_gap(final_scores$auc[final_scores$set == "train"],
                  final_scores$auc[final_scores$set == "test"], label = "AUC")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`finalize_workflow()` takes the workflow and the one-row tibble of chosen
values you printed on the line above.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
best_tree  <- select_best(tree_res, metric = "roc_auc")
best_tree

final_fit  <- finalize_workflow(tree_wf, best_tree) |> fit(data = train)
final_scores <- tree_scores(final_fit, "tuned")
final_scores
n_leaves(final_fit)

check_beats_prevalence(final_scores$accuracy[final_scores$set == "test"],
                       test$diabetes)
check_overfit_gap(final_scores$auc[final_scores$set == "train"],
                  final_scores$auc[final_scores$set == "test"], label = "AUC")
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
final_fit = search.______
f = tree_scores(final_fit, "tuned")
print(f)
print(final_fit.get_n_leaves())

check_beats_prevalence(f.loc[f["set"] == "test", "accuracy"].item(), y_te)
check_overfit_gap(f.loc[f["set"] == "train", "auc"].item(),
                  f.loc[f["set"] == "test", "auc"].item(), label="AUC")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`GridSearchCV` with `refit=True`, the default, has already refitted the winning
settings on the whole training set and stored the result on an attribute whose
name says so.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
final_fit = search.best_estimator_
f = tree_scores(final_fit, "tuned")
print(f)
print(final_fit.get_n_leaves())

check_beats_prevalence(f.loc[f["set"] == "test", "accuracy"].item(), y_te)
check_overfit_gap(f.loc[f["set"] == "train", "auc"].item(),
                  f.loc[f["set"] == "test", "auc"].item(), label="AUC")
```
:::
:::
:::

`check_overfit_gap` passes in R, where the tuned tree's train and test AUCs sit
within 0.01 of each other, and fails in Python, where the gap is about 0.13.
The grids are not identical and neither are the folds, so the two searches
landed on trees of different sizes — six leaves against sixteen. Tuning
narrows the gap; it does not guarantee to close it, and a check that fails is
reporting a fact about your model rather than a mistake in your code.

Finally, draw the tuned tree with the call from the first worked example. A
tree you can read aloud is worth more than two points of AUC in most clinical
settings.

## The result that should bother you

The unconstrained tree classifies every one of the 537 training patients
correctly. Its test accuracy is about 0.61–0.65, against a majority-class rule
that scores 0.636 with no data at all, and its test AUC is about 0.59–0.63,
against the shuffled-label spread you measured in @sec-classification-metrics.

Three steps.

1. Perfect training accuracy is not a strong result; it is the absence of a
   result. Any model with enough capacity can memorise 537 rows, and the one
   that does so carries no information beyond the rows themselves.
2. The failure is invisible from the training side. Nothing in the fit warns
   you. Only the held-out rows distinguish a tree that has learnt from a tree
   that has memorised, which is why the split from Day 1 is not an optional
   refinement.
3. The cure is less capacity, not more data cleaning or more predictors. The
   tuned tree has six leaves in R and sixteen in Python, rather than a hundred
   and more, loses nothing on the training rows that was worth keeping, and
   gains about fourteen points of test AUC.

And the comparison that should temper your enthusiasm for the tuned tree: the
logistic regression in @sec-classification-metrics reached a test AUC of
0.78–0.84 on the same split. The tuned tree reaches about 0.74–0.77. The
flexible model, properly tuned, is behind the straight line.

## Reflection

1. A colleague reports a decision tree with 99% accuracy and offers to show you
   the code. What do you ask for instead, and in what order?
2. The tuned tree has six leaves. Name one clinical advantage of that over a
   model with a hundred and thirty, that has nothing to do with accuracy.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values.** Resampling makes the tuned row move; quote ranges.

| | R, seed 123 | Python, random_state 123 |
|---|---|---|
| default tree: leaves | 10 (rpart prunes at cp = 0.01) | 110, depth 14 (grows to purity) |
| default tree: train / test accuracy | 0.795 / 0.753 | 1.000 / 0.61 |
| default tree: train / test AUC | 0.794 / 0.755 | 1.000 / 0.59 |
| unconstrained tree (R): leaves | 126 | — |
| unconstrained tree (R): train / test accuracy | 1.000 / 0.654 | — |
| depth 3, min_n 20: train / test accuracy | 0.762 / 0.749 | 0.765 / 0.727 |
| grid size | 27 points × 5 folds | 18 points × 5 folds |
| best resampled AUC | 0.74–0.75 | 0.77–0.78 |
| AUC across the whole grid | 0.645 to 0.742 | 0.720 to 0.779 |
| chosen settings | depth 6, `min_n` 22–40, cp 0.001–0.01 | depth 6, leaf 20, ccp 0.001 |
| tuned: test accuracy / AUC | 0.771 / 0.767 | 0.688 / 0.738 |
| tuned: train / test AUC gap | +0.01, passes `check_overfit_gap` | +0.13, fails it |
| tuned: leaves | 6 | 16 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[40,30,30]"}

Across four seeds for the fold assignment, R chose `tree_depth = 6` every
time and `min_n` between 22 and 40, with a resampled AUC of 0.743 to 0.753. If
a student's chosen `min_n` differs from the neighbour's, that is the exercise
working, not an error — it is worth saying so before anyone starts debugging.

**The cross-language gap is the set piece of this page.** Do not let it be
read as "R is better at trees". Put the two leaf counts on the board and ask
which default a student would have reported in a paper, and how a reader would
know.

**Common failures.** (1) `rpart.plot()` warning about `roundint` — it is
silenced with `roundint = FALSE`, which is already in the worked example; if a
student writes their own call they will meet it. (2) Tuning with
`resamples = test` or finalising before `select_best()`. (3) Expecting
`select_best()` to be reproducible across fold seeds; see above. (4) In Python,
calling `search.best_estimator_.fit()` again, which is unnecessary and resets
nothing useful.

**Timing.** The grid is deliberately small: 27 points by 5 folds runs in about
four seconds. If the room has spare time, widening `levels = 3` to `levels = 5`
is the right way to spend it; if the room is behind, drop Task 1.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — The one-standard-error rule
`select_by_one_std_err()` picks the simplest model whose performance is within
one standard error of the best. Apply it to `tree_res`, with
`desc(cost_complexity)` as the ordering, and compare the tree you get. Argue
for one of the two choices in a sentence a reviewer would accept.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — How stable is the tree itself?
Refit the default tree on five bootstrap resamples of the training rows and
draw each. The split at the root is usually the same variable; the splits three
levels down are usually not. What does that instability imply about reading a
single tree as an explanation of the disease?
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 3 — A tree on the length-of-stay data
`decision_tree(mode = "regression")` on `data/los_data.csv`, against the linear
model of @sec-regression-metrics. The tree loses, and the reason — a tree
predicts a constant within each leaf, so it cannot extrapolate a straight
relationship — is the same reason it won nothing here.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can fit, draw, deliberately break and then tune a decision
tree, and that you can tell the difference between a model that has learnt and
one that has memorised without looking at the test set more than once.

**Cannot:** that a tuned tree is a competitive model. It is not, here. Stretch 2
points at why — a single tree is unstable, and its instability is variance you
could average away. Averaging many unstable trees is @sec-random-forest.
